title: Khao Chang Hai Cave
intro: Explore the value of a living cave ecosystem, from biodiversity to community livelihoods.
research: Valuing ecosystem services and testing an integrated model for shared learning at Khao Chang Hai Cave, Trang Province.
overview: Human activities, including tourism, put limestone and cave ecosystems under pressure. This game helps local communities and stakeholders discuss biodiversity, ecosystem services and their economic value at Khao Chang Hai Cave in Trang.
materials: Forest-product, tree, animal and activity cards; an A2 board.
Ecosystem-service information sheets, pre/post tests, evaluation forms, answer sheets, a turn guide and a carbon-credit facilitator script.
Seven colours of tokens and beads, two dice, play money, role labels and a nine-piece elephant puzzle.
play: Assign community roles and distribute resources as specified in the source guide. Players collect biodiversity cards while working together to complete the elephant puzzle.
Roll the dice, move and follow the space instructions. Place animal beads in the appropriate habitat; remove them when an animal card is discarded. Keep tree and forest-product cards.

Complete two forest habitats with ten animal species each and seven cave chambers with three species each to collect nine puzzle pieces. Completing the puzzle ends the game; the player with the most biodiversity cards wins.

Passing the start marks one game year. At annual intervals, trade forest products, discuss carbon-credit registration and allocate role budgets. The usual activity spans two game years, adjustable by the facilitator.

In the second year, registered players can trade tree-based carbon credits. The facilitator introduces a carbon-tax scenario to explore emissions and offsets. Use the source tables for role budgets and detailed conditions.
learning: Connect tourism, forest products, biodiversity, carbon storage and community responsibilities. The source includes space-by-space learning points and discussion questions.
debrief: Discuss how ecosystem services support community income and wellbeing, how activities affect biodiversity, and which conservation and maintenance practices can sustain the cave ecosystem.

title: Soil Analysis & Fertilizer Use
intro: Make soil nutrients visible and learn why different fields need different decisions.
research: Game for Low-Formal Education Farmers to Learn How to Improve Soil Quality.
overview: Repeated cultivation and limited understanding of soil quality can contribute to degraded farmland and pressure on forests. SAAFU is a learning tool for soil sampling, fertilizer selection and discussion of farmers’ soil-management challenges.
materials: Pre/post tests; green, yellow, orange and pink beads; red, yellow and blue 4 × 4 cm foam pieces.
Paper clips, six-well plastic trays, 1-inch cassava cards and fertilizer bags for each player.
A sequence sheet, score board, fertilizer price table, fertilizer containers and a calculator.
play: Arrange 12–16 players in a U shape or small groups. This is a learning activity, not a competition. Begin with a pretest and introduce soil quality, lime and fertilizer formulas.
Distribute the source guide’s starting soil sets. Beads represent nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and lime; clips represent organic matter and foam represents soil pH.
Each six-well tray represents one rai. Players inspect their soil, plant cassava cards and buy fertilizer to meet the game’s crop requirements: N–P–K 22–4–29 and two units of organic matter per rai.
Check the crop and soil conditions. In the simulation cassava is sold after at least two years, with half-price sales when the specified conditions are not met.
Discuss nutrient uptake, leaching, fertilizer costs and income. Repeat for two rounds, then debrief and complete the posttest. Consult the source tables for starting sets, prices and soil conditions.
debrief: Compare outcomes across soils. Discuss why copying a neighbour’s fertilizer practice can produce different results, how soil analysis can avoid unnecessary expense, and how drought and other factors also affect soil quality. Keep the game’s learning purpose clear.

title: Thung Tha Ruea–Pak Phli
intro: Balance livelihoods and a shared wetland as water becomes scarce.
research: Studying wetland ecosystem services and community knowledge at Thung Yai Pak Phli, Nakhon Nayok, using Companion Modelling.
overview: This game supports shared learning about wetland ecosystem services and climate adaptation at Thung Tha Ruea–Pak Phli. Players explore how natural pressures and human activities affect the wetland and surrounding communities.
materials: Agricultural activity cards (4 × 4 cm), forest-product cards and scenario cards.
An A2 board, blue and orange beads, dice, pins and playing pieces.
Player record sheets, information tables and pre/post tests.
play: Pair 12 players into six pairs, divided into three resource levels with two pairs per level. Land endowments and goals differ; use the source table.
After a pretest, choose farming, water use, chemical use and forest-product collection activities and record decisions. Water is sufficient for everyone in the first year.
Roll, move and follow board instructions. A player passing the starting space marks one year. Pause for discussion after the first round.
For the second round, introduce reduced rainfall and additional upstream users. Continue play while facilitators observe adaptation and negotiation.
After two rounds, complete the posttest and discuss the outcomes.
debrief: Compare how land resources, water availability and economic choices affect incomes. Discuss water negotiation, forest-product collection, drought, floods, climate change and outside users, then connect planning decisions to wetland conservation.

title: Herptile ESs
intro: Discover the ecological roles of amphibians and reptiles in agricultural landscapes.
research: Gaming and simulation for learning about amphibian and reptile ecosystem services in agricultural ecosystems in Nan Province.
overview: Agricultural chemicals, forest burning and other human activities threaten amphibian and reptile diversity. Herptile ESs makes their benefits, relationships and vulnerability visible and creates a space for participants to discuss conservation.
materials: Habitat diagrams; amphibian and reptile cards (5.5 × 8.6 cm); question and event cards.
An A2 board, six colours of pins, playing pieces and dice.
Pre/post tests and the game manual.
play: Seat 4–6 players around a board. Agree the duration with the facilitator. Each player receives twenty pins of one colour and a playing piece.
Roll to select a starting player and agree a direction of play. Learn to read species cards, habitat symbols and the board using the source guide.
Move around the board and follow its instructions, answer questions and resolve events. Relate species to their habitats and ecosystem roles.

At conservation spaces, suggest ways to protect amphibians and reptiles. Finish with a shared learning summary and the assessment activities. Use the source tables for detailed card effects and conditions.
debrief: Discuss amphibian and reptile diversity, the ecosystem services these animals provide and the effects of farming and chemicals. Connect observations in play to practical conservation and the role of species as biological indicators.

title: Farmer versus Climate Change
intro: Adapt a farm through heavy rain, drought and changing agricultural conditions.
research: Gaming and simulation for learning about climate adaptation in agricultural ecosystems in Nan Province.
overview: Farmers face drought, heavy rainfall and other climate pressures, while land clearing can contribute to flooding and landslides. This game explores the relationship between agriculture and climate change and helps participants exchange adaptation strategies.
materials: Agricultural activity, fertilizer/pesticide, profit-focused and adaptation cards; reservoir and firebreak pieces.
A 61.5 × 76 cm board with 5.1 × 5 cm spaces, play money, tokens, coloured labels, buttons and containers.
Price sheets, recording forms, pre/post tests, evaluation forms and a manual.
play: Form groups of 4–5 players, complete a pretest, distribute starting resources and explain the rules.
Place tokens on farmland. Choose agricultural activities, fertilizers, pesticides and adaptation options, following the source’s purchase limits. Place the cards and record decisions.

The facilitator tracks collective greenhouse-gas emissions. In this simulation, totals of 250 and 500 units reduce crop sale prices by 1,000 and 2,000 baht per rai respectively; wildfire reduces affected crop prices to zero.
Resolve five rounds: normal conditions, heavy rain, drought, increased pests and weeds, then drought. Calculate crop income at the end of each round.
Before the next round, choose whether to incorporate crop residues into the soil or burn them. Complete five rounds, or adjust to the session, then debrief and take the posttest.
debrief: Use questions and shared responses to discuss climate causes and impacts, adaptation, agriculture–climate interactions, market shortages and surpluses, chemical contamination and bio-sentinel species.

title: Community Forest no CanCel
intro: Work together to keep a community forest productive, resilient and valuable.
research: Gaming and simulation for learning about community forest ecosystem services and sustainable management.
overview: CF no CC was developed particularly for young people in Nan. It explores provisioning, regulating and cultural services while practising collective decisions, planning and sustainable resource management under climate variability.
materials: Tree, product, building, activity and character cards, with their conditions.
A 54 × 36 cm board, coloured paper, play banknotes and certificates.
Event descriptions, pre/post tests and recording sheets for harvesting, activity planning and income.
play: Prepare a table and presentation screen. Randomly place five tree cards and the initial forest-product cards. Divide participants into at least two equally sized groups with one facilitator per table.
Allow ten minutes for the pretest. Explain forest ecosystem services, then guide the first round. Distribute character cards, money, paper clips and coloured paper.
Players choose to collect two forest-product cards or take one learning card. Record the choice. Present five activity cards and let players discuss costs, participation and impacts.
Players can exchange learning and products for a business card according to its conditions. Pay activity costs and place buildings where required.
Sell products, operate businesses and receive activity income; activities pay in the following round. Announce an event and replenish products according to their conditions.
Play for up to seven rounds or the available time. Compare forests and mission completion, then allow ten minutes for the posttest and satisfaction assessment.
debrief: Reflect on resource choices, their consequences and the three groups of forest ecosystem services. Compare cooperation across groups and discuss sustainable management under climate change. Collect feedback for improving the activity.

title: Diversity at Lai Nan
intro: Meet local trees, birds, insects and fungi—and connect them into a food web.
research: The research-title field is blank in the supplied document.
overview: Research in community forests at Lai Nan, Wiang Sa District, Nan, found high biological diversity. This card-based model uses those findings to help local people recognise and learn about their own natural resources.
materials: Resource cards representing trees, birds, insects and fungi.
Forest-abundance level cards, question cards and a game manual.
play: Give each player five resource cards and begin with a level-one forest. Track how many resource cards have been played.
Choose the first player and continue to the right. Play one resource or tree card at a time, read its name and ability, apply the effect and calculate points.

Use the requirements printed on each card. Forest levels represent different capacities to support organisms. Moving from level one to two requires twenty resource cards; moving from two to three requires forty.
Explore questions about trees, birds, insects, mushrooms and community forests. Card symbols explain organism size, diet and ecological roles. The source does not specify group size or duration.
debrief: Ask participants what they learned and which organisms interested them. Draw arrows between familiar organisms to create a food web, then discuss producers, consumers, decomposers and the benefits people receive from forests.

title: Manage-For-Nan
intro: Bring villagers and forest managers together to plan a thriving planted forest.
research: Assessing ecosystem services and testing a participatory integrated model for planted-forest management in Nan Province.
overview: Manage-For-Nan is a three-dimensional role-playing board game that makes planted-forest ecosystem services visible. Participants share knowledge and develop forest-management plans suited to their local community.
materials: A 420-cell landscape board (20 × 21), with each cell representing one rai; land-cover pieces and pins.
Forest-product, bird, pavilion and six event cards covering normal conditions, recession, drought and unseasonal rainfall.
Role and income records, planting and crop cost/price sheets, play money, labour tokens and wildfire beads.
An Excel recording/results file and pre/post learning assessments are listed in the source; no separate spreadsheet was supplied.
play: Assign one university regional learning-centre officer and 5–10 villagers. The officer aims for 80 rai of planted forest, including 20 rai at level three, over five rounds with an annual budget of 200,000 baht.
Villagers seek the highest cumulative income from farming and forest products. Each has ten rai and starting capital of 30,000 or 50,000 baht; they can also plant and maintain forest.
Explain the roles and scenario. In scenario two, negotiate joint agreements before selecting activities.
Choose farming, collection, planting and maintenance activities; allocate labour and record costs. Resolve special activities such as birdwatching, school projects, research and pavilion placement.
Draw wildfire and event outcomes, calculate income and ecosystem-service benefits, update records and the board, and continue for five rounds.
debrief: Compare villagers’ and officers’ experiences. Discuss provisioning, regulating and cultural services, shared project planning, planting and ongoing care. Consider wildfire, drought and economic risks when designing a management plan for the community.

title: Coco Green Space
intro: Co-design urban green spaces that serve people, birds and a shared future.
research: Gaming and simulation for shared learning about the importance and co-construction of urban green space.
overview: Urban growth can reduce green space and worsen biodiversity loss, heat, air pollution and wellbeing. This game helps community roles explore six green-space types, agree shared benefits and negotiate the trade-offs involved in creating useful, lasting green spaces.
materials: A 200-cell board with 6 × 6 cm cells; nine role tokens; green-space and other land-use pictograms.
Recording and purchase sheets; five scenario cards; sixteen co-benefit types; bird habitat condition cards.
Activity and knowledge cards, fish/forest-product/bird tokens, orange carbon beads, certificates, pre/post tests and satisfaction forms.
The source also lists an Excel income/results file; no separate spreadsheet was supplied.
play: Use nine players per group, ideally two groups for comparison. Assign teacher, student, local authority, factory, health centre, farmer, monk, bird and environmentalist roles. Complete a five-minute pretest.
Agree three shared co-benefits. Allow three minutes to plan green-space purchases and discuss joint development.
Roles one to seven purchase and place green-space pictograms in turn. The bird player places birds according to habitat conditions; the environmentalist records biodiversity and benefits.
Plan two public activities, pay the game’s participation costs, exchange knowledge and award certificates. Photograph the board, place carbon beads representing absorption and pay income.

Introduce the remaining climate, tourism, pollution and funding scenarios, recording carbon and outcomes. The design includes five scenarios; the documented trial used approximately two hours for three rounds.
Finish with a five-minute posttest, a satisfaction assessment and a group debrief.
debrief: Compare the two groups’ boards and strategies. Use carbon-bead totals and available results to discuss emissions and absorption. Examine birds as indicators of green-space quality, then agree desired co-benefits and co-design a real pilot green space.

title: Green Roof Bingo
intro: Design a rooftop landscape and discover the ecosystem services it can provide.
research: Board game for collective learning on green roof ecosystem services.
overview: Green roofs can add vegetation to existing buildings where ground-level green space is limited. Players act as building owners, designing roofs within a budget and exploring provisioning, habitat, regulating and cultural services through bingo and redesign.
materials: Individual 25-cell roof boards and roof-component pieces, including vegetation, ground surfaces, water and facilities.
Numbered ecosystem-service condition cards (1–24), bingo materials, component descriptions and cost information.
Roof recording sheets, assessments of four ecosystem-service groups, pre/post tests and satisfaction forms. Detailed component quantities and illustrations are in the original source.
play: Prepare 8–12 building-owner roles with equal starting funds and individual 25-cell boards. Introduce green roofs and complete the pretest.
In round one, draw building locations A–H and spend 10–20 minutes filling the board with selected components within the budget. Record the roof design.
Draw numbers 1–24 and read their ecosystem-service conditions. Players whose roofs qualify mark the corresponding number. Five aligned marks earn a bingo bonus.
The first round ends when one player completes three bingo lines. Add component service scores and bingo bonuses, then discuss the design choices.
In round two, redesign the roofs using what was learned and assess all four service groups. The highest total wins, with an additional award for the greatest improvement.

Use approximately thirty minutes per round. Discuss context-specific building load and public-access conditions; in this game bees require at least four flowering-plant cells. Complete the posttest and satisfaction assessment.
debrief: Walk around the roof designs and compare components, costs and services. Discuss carbon storage, shade, runoff, food, income, habitat and recreation. Compare scores between rounds and explore how roofs can act as habitat stepping stones and inspire local green-space projects.

title: NEST
intro: See the city through a bird’s eyes and make room for the next generation.
research: Ecological factors on bird nest site selection and integrative model for bird conservation in urban green space. Master’s thesis in Zoology, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, academic year 2025 (2568 BE), by เอื้อการย์ ทองโชติ.
overview: NEST (Nesting Ecology and the Selection of Trees) uses Companion Modelling to explore urban bird conservation. A campus survey from April 2024 to March 2025 recorded 182 nests in four nest categories on 124 trees of twenty species. Players take gardener, bird and birdwatcher roles to negotiate tree management and nesting needs. The source describes three versions used with young people, university students and green-space stakeholders.
materials: A 54 × 54 cm, 43-cell board: twelve rain-tree, nine pradu, six pink trumpet-tree, four copperpod, five building and seven empty cells.
Tree models with a trunk, two main branches and two small branches; bird and egg pieces for five bird species.
Six situation cards and six building-activity cards; role, goal and placement-condition sheets.
Gardener and birdwatcher records, scoring criteria, a ten-question pre/post test, an eleven-item model assessment, clay, bottle caps and fruit picks.
play: Assign 12–14 participants to gardeners/facilities staff, five bird species and birdwatchers, with 1–2 people per role. Provide one facilitator per seven players and allow 90–150 minutes.
Complete the pretest and explain role goals and placement conditions. Play six rounds, each representing two months.
Draw a situation card and place activity cards on buildings. Gardeners can take up to ten pruning/planting actions, with pruning restricted to trees around active buildings.

Birds place themselves and eggs according to species-specific rounds, tree/branch conditions and distance from buildings. Near-building nests earn one egg and farther nests earn two under the game rules.

Birdwatchers count eggs and occupied trees and score the site. A total below five reduces the gardener’s next-round actions by one. Before round four, add small branches to trees that retain main branches.

After six rounds, check each role’s goals. Gardeners aim to prune at least sixty branches and plant at least as many replacement trees as the first-round tree count; birds have species-specific egg goals. Debrief and complete the posttest and assessment.
debrief: Let each role explain successes and obstacles. Discuss tree species, branches, canopy, building distance, nest types, pruning and disturbance. Explore negotiation and possible local actions such as protecting occupied branches, nesting boxes, diverse green spaces and quieter conservation areas.
